speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRIME MINISTER OF TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to call your attention and the attention of members of the house to the presence in the Speaker's gallery of the right hon. Prime Minister of Trinidad and Tobago, Dr. Williams, members of his cabinet, the high commissioner and staff members.
I am sure all members of this house will wish to give the warmest possible welcome to Dr. Williams and his party.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRIME MINISTER OF TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRIME MINISTER OF TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO
speechtext:
We welcome the Prime Minister, not only as prime minister but as one who has achieved great personal distinction in the fields of scholarship, of education and international service as well as politics. We welcome him as the dynamic leader of a new, dynamic free state in the Caribbean and in the commonwealth of nations. Canada has long had warm and friendly contacts with Trinidad and Tobago and with the British Caribbean colonies, some of which are now independent states in the commonwealth, and it is our policy to strengthen those contacts in every way possible. I believe that the visit of our friends from Trinidad and Tobago will be helpful in that respect.
I hope their stay in Canada, though short, will be a pleasant one. I am confident that it will promote even closer co-operation between our two countries in the commonwealth of nations.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRIME MINISTER OF TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of ihe Opposition):
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRIME MINISTER OF TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join the right hon. Prime Minister in welcoming the right hon. Prime Minister of Trinidad and Tobago. Indeed, it is rather an unusual occasion when two members of Her Majesty's privy council welcome a third member on Her Majesty's birthday. It emphasizes something of the importance, alluded to by the Prime Minister, of the commonwealth relationship.
Indeed, as one who through the years has been an avowed follower of the commonwealth principle, it is well that prime ministers of various parts of the commonwealth should meet together. I was attending the prime ministers' conference when the right hon. Prime Minister of Trinidad and Tobago made his initial appearance there. He is one who has given outstanding leadership in his country; one who all of us are proud to recognize as a leader of one of the newer members of the commonwealth and one of the older in the old empire. He comes with a mission, one that will receive the support of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition. We believe that the commonwealth should be strengthened in every way possible and that every assistance that the older members of the commonwealth can give to the newer members to start them along the road to economic strength will be acceptable to all members of the commonwealth.
I join with the Prime Minister in welcoming not only Dr. Williams but also the members of his cabinet who are with him. Through you, Mr. Speaker, I wish to assure the people of Trinidad and Tobago that the Canadian people are proud to be associated with a nation with so traditionally fine a democratic history.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRIME MINISTER OF TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of this party wish to associate themselves with the remarks of the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition in extending a word of welcome to the right hon. Dr. Williams, Prime Minister of Trinidad and Tobago, and the party accompanying him here today. We are pleased to have them here in Canada, and we trust that their visit will make for a closer relationship between our respective countries.
We in this party have been urging throughout the years that Canada take a more active part in promoting economic development programs, particularly in less developed areas of the world. Instead of scattering our assistance over a wide area it has often seemed to me that one of the most effective things we could do would be for Canada to adopt the Caribbean area, and particularly that part of the Caribbean area that is in the commonwealth. We have common interests and a common adherence to parliamentary institutions, and we could work closely together to help develop that area. I trust that the visit of the Prime

Visitors in Gallery
Minister of Trinidad and Tobago will lay the foundation for such a program of mutual help and assistance.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRIME MINISTER OF TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with genuine pleasure that we join the entire membership of this house in welcoming the right hon. Prime Minister of Trinidad and Tobago, Dr. Williams, and the members of his party who are with him. As one who is personally familiar with the general Caribbean area I can say that the friendly relationships which are now developing again in a more intensive way between Canada and our sister commonwealth countries in the Caribbean area are not only a challenge but a means of strengthening our dual roles in this western hemisphere. My mind goes back to the days when the "Lady" boats did so much to bring us closer together, and now with air connections established we are within a few hours journey of each other. Certainly the neighbourly responsibilities and friendships which exist between us can be developed in the immediate years ahead to a greater potential than ever before.
Therefore we welcome the presence of our distinguished friends and neighbours with us here this afternoon and trust that their visit will be one of much benefit.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRIME MINISTER OF TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we wish to join with the other members of the house to extend the warmest welcome to the Prime Minister of Trinidad and Tobago.
There is talk about trade between the commonwealth countries. Well, trade relations with that country in particular can be very warm because it is a land of bright sunshine and beautiful waters, especially during those months when snow is plentiful in our own country.
Such trade could benefit our two countries. I feel that today in particular the understanding between the countries of the British commonwealth, which work together to maintain peaceful and friendly relations, can set an example to the other countries and make it easier for the whole world to achieve the understanding and harmony which exist within the commonwealth.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF DATE OF MEETING OF PRIME MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition has reminded us that this is Her Majesty's birthday. In joining as I am sure we all do in good wishes and congratulations on this day and the old desire for many happy returns, it seems appropriate that I should be in a position to make an announcement regarding a meeting of commonwealth prime ministers in London.
Hon. members will recall that after the visit to Ottawa of the British prime minister in mid February I said that we had had some talks about the possibility of a commonwealth prime ministers' meeting some time next summer. On March 30 I informed the house of my understanding that formal invitations for such a meeting were being sent out. It has now been agreed by all concerned-with one exception, Zanzibar, which has not yet replied-that the meeting should take place from July 8 to July 15. An announcement to this effect is also being made today in the British parliament in London.

subtopic: TRANSFER OF HOSPITALS FROM FEDERAL CONTROL
TRANSFER OF HOSPITALS FROM FEDERAL CONTROL
speechtext:
When the house adjourned at ten o'clock last night I was speaking on the amendment to the supply motion with regard to the take-over by provincial or other authorities of the D.V.A. hospitals. I was making three points.
Veterans Hospitals Transfer
The first was that the minister gave an undertaking that before any change in the control or use of these hospitals was brought about this whole matter would be referred to the standing committee on veterans affairs. Second, his undertaking was that before any change was made in this regard he would refer the matter to the veterans associations both provincial and federal.
I now charge the minister with having misled not only the house but the public in this regard, and I say this because in the first place, the matter has not been referred to the standing committee on veterans affairs and, in the second place, he has not consulted with the federal president of the Legion or with other veterans organizations. I hold in my hand an article which appeared in the Calgary Herald of April 16 last stating that the Colonel Belcher hospital auxiliary association has asked the minister for a definite statement of policy on the future use of military hospitals and expressed its alarm, in a letter to the minister over this proposal to reorganize veterans hospital services.
I wish to make our position clear. Our position is hands off these hospitals. The position taken by hon. gentlemen opposite appears to be "Hands on these hospitals but keep the matter secret". We have heard talk lately about the new open diplomacy. Does the government intend to come forward in the last 24 hours and say it has only been negotiating as far as this question is concerned? Is this in accordance with the new point of view about open diplomacy?
I say to the minister that he has an obligation to the House of Commons and to every veteran in Canada to come clean on this subject and tell us where his government stands on this matter. Judging by the answers he has given to questions so far, he knows that during the last two months there have been negotiations under way with reference to transferring control of these hospitals to the provincial or municipal level. I charge him again with having been wishy-washy in his answers and in his decisions with reference to this subject. In fact there is a conflict between the position he took and the position taken by the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister assured us that there would be no change in control. If it turns out that this means that the title is to remain with the department though the actual use goes to the provinces, if this is what "no change in control" means, I think we are merely playing with words. The house and the country are entitled to know what is taking place. I charge the minister with deliberately deceiving the veterans in this regard.

Mr. Speaker, it is certainly not my intention this afternoon to engage in a debate the like of which we have just heard. I think this subject is much too important for that, and I have serious doubts about anyone who suggests that any other member of this house would act with any intent to deceive either the House of Commons or the veterans of Canada.
The mover of this amendment yesterday repeatedly stated that a serious problem did exist in the administration of our D.V.A. hospitals. In fact he admitted that as far back as 1959 there was a recognition of this developing problem. I believe he said that when he was minister he decided to wait for the report of the Glassco commission before making a decision. As a result of that report he stated then, as was stated a few minutes ago by the hon. member for Bow River, that the policy was hands off the D.V.A. hospitals. I think that is a clearcut statement, and I do not quarrel with it.
However, all hon. members who are familiar with the hearings before the veterans affairs committee last year and all those who have spoken in this debate recognize that there is a serious problem in the administration of these hospitals. I do not intend to debate that fact, because I believe we can take it that the existence of the problem has been recognized. The mover of the amendment recognized it. The hon. member for Kootenay West recognized it. Perhaps I might also quote from the report which the committee made last year; this is recommendation number 12:
Your committee is aware that a point has been reached where a decision must be made regarding treatment service in both areas of responsibility and administration.
Your committee recommends that the fullest consultation be carried out with veterans organizations before any changes are made.
I think it may be useful at this stage to outline what the problem is. It is one which has been developing because of the increasing case load in our hospitals of long term and chronic illness with the result that we are no longer able to bring to bear on the treatment of veterans in our hospitals the kind of medical services which are available to the general community outside. This is aggravated, of course, by the fact that there is a shortage of professional staff throughout the country, and when medical people and nurses have a choice between our hospitals and others they naturally gravitate to those hospitals which can offer the broadest opportunities.
Among other things that have occurred is this. The Royal College of Physicians have [Mr. Woolliams.l
downgraded our hospitals in terms of facilities for teaching. Ten years ago a large number of medical people graduated after taking three year courses at our hospitals, but these facilities have now been downgraded because the case load at our hospitals does not supply the kind of cases which are of interest to professionals. Thus we are faced with circumstances which will prevent us, if our hospitals remain as they are, from providing for the veteran population the kind of medical treatment which every one of us would agree our veterans are entitled to receive.
So, facing this problem, what do we do about it? I do not think there is any point in saying that we just carry on. That was one of the alternatives, among many, that we faced. What do we do about this? How do we face this problem? Certainly one of the alternatives is "Do nothing; we will just carry on this way". Another alternative was certainly the recommendation of the Glassco commission. But if we read the recommendation of the Glassco commission, what does it recommend? It recommends that we gradually move our veteran patients from the hospitals, and its final recommendation reads as follows:
Active treatment hospitals now operated by the Department of Veterans Affairs, when cleared, be sold and converted into community hospitals under transfer agreements providing preferential admission rights for veterans with pensionable disabilities.
I can understand why the previous minister turned that down, because that recommendation is unacceptable; it would be impossible to really do a job of work. In effect it would mean a continuation of the downgrading of our hospitals until we moved our veteran patients elsewhere, and then ridding ourselves of the buildings.
Another alternative has been suggested. It is curious to note, Mr. Speaker, that in all the letters I have received, with the exception of two or three very thoughtful letters, the central problem was ignored. In some of these thoughtful letters it was said-and I have heard others make this recommendation -we could have opened our doors to the general public and therefore have brought into these hospitals the kind of patient case load which would enable us to bring into the hospitals the kind of medical people, professional staff, that would enable us to discharge our responsibilities adequately. That was an alternative that was looked at, but here we were moving into an area where constitutional difficulties would have arisen, because we would be moving into a strictly provincial field. The administration of hospitals is not within the prerogative of the federal government. There is no question about operating

our veterans hospitals; that is recognized and accepted, but the operation of hospitals for the general community is a provincial matter. I think we must accept and recognize that, particularly in the climate of today, we would have invited a controversy and difficulties here which would have made the treatment of our veterans even more difficult.
Then, of course, there was another alternative that suggested itself. That was the alternative I spoke of in the statement I made the other day; that where possible, and with adequate safeguards, we might be able to reach agreement with appropriate authorities whereby we would transfer the operation of a hospital into what I will call, for want of a better word, civilian hands; whereby we could have available in that hospital the highest possible standard of medical treatment that was available in the community; and within that hospital guarantee for ourselves enough space and beds to ensure that the department would carry out its responsibilities. In the statement I gave to the house the other day I laid down several conditions. I said:
At this point I would like to make it unequivocally and emphatically clear that no such agreements will be entered into by the government unless certain sine Qua non conditions are met. These conditions.. .are as follows: First, accommodation for the treatment of service connected disabilities among veterans must be immediately available at all times, and treatment must be provided in accordance with standards prescribed by the Department of Veterans Affairs.
We have some experience in this field. We have a situation in Saskatoon, for instance, where this exists; where the federal government made a grant to the university hospital and where enough beds are reserved with top priority for the Department of Veterans Affairs in order that it may discharge its duties. I do not think anyone will complain about the kind of treatment our veterans are receiving in that hospital. There is space provided for our people within the hospital and this, of course, we would ensure. We would have to have an absolute the premises, in order that the veterans Affairs would decide who should be admitted to the priority beds, when they would be discharged. Our staff would be available on the premises, in order that the veterans would report to the Department of Veterans Affairs staff. In other words we would retain complete and thorough control of the treatment of our veterans.

This actually happens in Saskatoon; it works, and we know it works. The agreement is respected. I suggest to the house that in this instance we have the best medical service available to our veterans that is available to the community of Saskatoon. What is being suggested here is that people with whom we enter into an agreement are not responsible enough to respect it. I am sure that is not really a responsible statement, because we have experience of this kind of thing. We are not going to enter into an agreement with any group or body that is unreliable or will not respect the agreement that is entered into.
I would like to recall that when I made the statement the other day I also said this:
It is therefore the view of this government that the operational control of veterans hospitals should be transferred to non-federal agencies at times, in places, and under conditions which will best protect the standards of care to which veterans are entitled.
I readily admit that one of the difficulties that exists in this area is that the problem is quite different with each of the areas in Canada where hospitals are situated, and it is impossible to prescribe a set series of conditions which would apply in all cases. In this context, Mr. Speaker, may I say this regarding my agreeing to accept and respect the recommendations of the committee with respect to consultation with veterans organizations. It has seemed to me that rather than consulting, say, the dominion command or the veterans affairs committee in Ottawa we would be in a much better position if we were to consult the veterans who best know the area involved. In this instance I suggest we consult the veterans in the provincial command, who would best know the area, the conditions and the circumstances. In that regard I very much doubt whether in all the circumstances it will be possible to consult with the entire groupings, as I suggested previously, but we can certainly

Veterans Hospitals Transfer talk to the provincial command in the area of the hospital under discussion at the moment. That is a perfectly valid point, and we have undertaken to respect that recommendation. I interpret it in that light because surely that is where we will receive the best advice.
The question of when this consultation will take place is again a pretty difficult one, because until we reach the stage where we have a series of concrete proposals with conditions laid down and a draft document prepared, so that we can answer the questions which will be asked and have something specific to go on, I do not think we are in a position to consult intelligently.
As I indicated when answering questions in the course of my earlier statements, we have had proposals from a number of authorities. These are people who have written to us and suggested that they think they could meet the conditions that we have laid down. Before going further with the matter it would be necessary for my officials to take a look at the situation which these people were proposing. It would be necessary for these authorities to meet and discuss the details of the conditions we would require, so that we would be in a position to discuss more intelligently with the veterans organizations what we proposed to do.
I repeat, because I think it is extremely important, that it is my view that the standard of care to which veterans are entitled must be maintained, and that is the whole objective of this exercise, and we will retain control. In the one instance, that is true, that we have reached the stage where we are preparing the draft of an agreement in order to see whether these people are prepared to meet conditions which will satisfy us.

subtopic: TRANSFER OF HOSPITALS FROM FEDERAL CONTROL
speechtext: In view of the statement of the minister, a statement I have heard repeated and about which there has been some argument on that side of the house, why is it that I repeatedly run into cases-I am speaking of my personal experience in this matter -of veterans who are sent to Shaughnessy from the interior because they are told they can get better treatment for their disability there than they can at the local hospital? I have had one case brought to my attention this week.

subtopic: TRANSFER OF HOSPITALS FROM FEDERAL CONTROL
speechtext:
That is true in many of our hospitals today, but this is the standard which we want to maintain. Unfortunately this high standard is not true of all our hospitals, but in many of our hospitals today we still have a very high quality medical service. I thank my hon. friend for asking me that question, because it does permit me to underline the fact that we still have excellent staff in our hospitals. But recruiting is becoming more and more difficult, and before we reach the stage where that standard has deteriorated we feel we should take whatever action is necessary in order to put an end to the deterioration which we see coming in the near future.
While I am on that subject perhaps I might remove another misunderstanding with regard to the so-called empty beds in our hospitals. With very minor exceptions-and those exceptions are a result of staff problems-our hospitals are carrying patients at a capacity which is considered normal for a hospital. Our case loads run at an average of 75 per cent to 80 per cent capacity. So it is not a question of empty beds; it is a matter of the kind of patient we have in our hospitals. That is where the difficulty lies. We have a large percentage of chronic, long term care cases; in fact the average across the country of that type of case now runs to about 75 per cent, and therein lies our problem. Before any decision is taken, quite apart from the treatment factor involved, we have to make very sure that the veterans now in those hospitals and others who may come after them-long term, chronic cases-have adequate attention and facilities. That is another complicating factor. We must make sure that these people are looked after. They need medical attention. They do not need active treatment, but they do need medical attention.
Therefore-and this was the second condition in the statement I made the other day- we must assure ourselves that these facilities

are both in existence and are available to us. The hon. member who moved this amendment referred to construction programs last year. In Saskatoon we are providing this kind of facilities so as to make sure these people are looked after and removed from the kind of buildings in which they are presently housed; and that program is continuing. If hon. members were to study each case across Canada they would find there are as many variations in conditions as there are hospitals, and in some cases it will be many years before community resources are adequate to meet those conditions. We may have to make temporary arrangements in order to make available a full treatment program in such communities and to provide such facilities in our hospitals. This means that it will not be possible for me or for anybody else to set a specific standard which will apply to all our hospitals. We will have to deal with each one on its merits. We will have to study local circumstances and resources and the kind of arrangement that we should enter into.
There is another factor, which is not a negligible one and which I also mentioned, hon. members will recall, in my statement the other day. We have in these hospitals at the moment dedicated nurses and dedicated medical men, who are dedicated principally because they are veterans themselves. They are doing an excellent job of servicing these hospitals. While it is difficult to replace them, I think the Department of Veterans Affairs owes them some safeguard as well. We must make sure, given these conditions, that these people are adequately looked after.
Now, Mr. Speaker, to come to the amendment itself I find that it reads in part as follows:
This house deplores the announced decision of the government to abandon its responsibilities for the administration of veterans hospitals-
What we are being asked to do, and most of the letters I have received make the same request, is to ignore the problem; do not do anything. Hands off.

I think, on the contrary, what we have tried to do has been to face the problem. What do we do about it? Do we let our veteran population take second class medical treatment in the years ahead or do we say to ourselves that our first responsibility is not necessarily to maintain buildings for our people, but our first responsibility is to ensure that they get the care which Canadians want them to have?

Mr. Speaker, the argument which the minister has just completed revolved around the possibility of veterans treatment services deteriorating at some time in the future. Mark you, he referred only to the possibility, and adduced no facts to support that argument. I will come back a bit later to the various points he made in regard to medical treatment.
Before doing that I should like to go on and make a few points, particularly one related to something the minister said shortly before he sat down, and something along the same line which was said by the parliamentary secretary to the minister yesterday. They said that the introduction of this motion meant the introduction of partisanship in the consideration of veterans affairs, something which has not been done before. I feel that both the minister and his parliamentary secretary fail to realize that our inability


during the past several weeks and the inability of veterans organizations to find out what government policy was in regard to veterans hospitals, to find out what course of action is to be followed by the government, has left those of us concerned with the welfare of veterans and veterans hospitals with no alternative but to bring up this matter in this way.
This is the only means open to us at the present time by which we can have a full discussion of this matter. We would be failing in our responsibility to the veterans and for the veterans if we did not take this means of bringing the whole matter into the open.
I think I should make it clear that the amendment before the house has been moved because of the serious concern that veterans hospital services are to be reduced to the detriment of Canadian veterans. That is the reason the amendment was moved, because of real concern in that regard not only on the part of members of this and other parties in the House of Commons but also very real concern on the part of veterans and veterans organizations throughout Canada.
This fear on the part of veterans and their organizations first arose out of newspaper stories that the Colonel Belcher hospital in Calgary was to be turned over to civic or provincial authorities for operation. Their fear over what was going to happen to their hospital facilities and the hospital treatment to which they had become accustomed has progressively increased because of the indefinite and evasive answers which the minister has given to questions of all kinds during the past few weeks concerning the policy of the government.
Since the session started a long series of questions has been asked regarding this matter, but throughout the government has refused to say that a change in policy with regard to D.V.A. hospitals has been decided upon. They have refused throughout to admit definitely that they have decided on a change of policy, in spite of specific questions on that very point, put by myself and others to the minister in the house. Nevertheless, discussions with regard to Colonel Belcher hospital have continued, quite evidently with a view to turning it over to the civic and provincial authorities. In addition, civic and provincial authorities have made a succession of statements to the newspapers in Calgary indicating the number of beds they are going to secure by means of this deal, the number of operating rooms which are going to be made available to them and so forth.
All of this, combined with the evasive answers of the minister, has made it clear to

most people, I think, that in effect a change in policy was accepted by the government at one time. The replies of the Prime Minister in answer to questions asked him have already been referred to. I will not take the time of the house to repeat them at this moment, but he did give the impression that no change was to be made. In other words he gave the impression that previous statements made by the minister and by civic and provincial authorities in Alberta were not correct, and that the control and operation of Colonel Belcher hospital and other veterans hospitals were going to remain in the hands of the Department of Veterans Affairs.
So strongly was this impression given that I advised several of my correspondents that in view of what the Prime Minister had said I thought our fears with regard to what was going to happen to the Colonel Belcher hospital could be set at rest. Then, of course, subsequent answers given by the Minister of Veterans Affairs were to the exactly opposite effect, with the result that the whole question was up in the air again. We now have a picture of confusion, and the matter can only be cleared up by a definite statement of policy on the part of the government as to the course of action they are going to pursue.
We have not yet had such a statement. In anything the minister has said there has really been nothing definite with regard to what the policy is going to be. He has continued to talk about the situation prevailing in one part of Canada being different from that prevailing in another, but he still refuses to admit that the government, as now appears clear, has made a change in policy and is progressively going to turn over the operation of the D.V.A. hospitals to civilian control.
There has been another very bad result arising from the confusion which has existed and the conflicting statements that have been made. In particular, because of the indefinite and evasive statements of the Minister of Veterans Affairs, a lack of confidence in the minister has developed on the part of veterans and veterans organizations. In the past veterans organizations and veterans generally have looked to the minister of veterans affairs, whoever he may have been, as their representative in the cabinet and the defender of their interests, the person to whom they could turn for general support because as far as the government was concerned the general welfare of veterans was in his hands. This situation has very definitely changed. The result is that at the present time most veterans and veterans organizations have now come to look upon the minister as the leader in a movement to decrease or eliminate their hospital and treatment benefits and guarantees.

Several times during the past few weeks I have asked that the whole matter of future policy with regard to veterans hospitals be referred to the veterans affairs committee. On every occasion the minister has refused to say that this would be done. I ask why. Why does he refuse to say that the matter will be considered by the veterans affairs committee? Surely this is the body best fitted to consider the whole question of veterans hospitals. In other words, the matter could be thoroughly examined in that committee, and I do not know anywhere else where it can be thoroughly examined publicly and all the facts in connection with the matter brought out.
Surely it is essential that this be done so that members of the house and veterans and veterans organizations may be satisfied that the right course of action is being followed. Again I ask the question, why do the minister and the government refuse to have this matter considered and recommendations made thereon by the veterans affairs committee, the only place where the matter can be thoroughly aired?
The minister and his parliamentary secretary both continue to reiterate that their great concern is to safeguard the interests and welfare of the veterans. Once more I ask, if that is the case why do they not take the obvious step to ensure that this will be done, by referring the matter to the committee rather than refusing to have it thoroughly investigated? I would strongly urge on the minister and the government that they take this action now. The veterans affairs committee has been set up and had its first meeting this morning. I did not intend to take part in this debate but I should like to say a few words now on the amendment which has been moved.
I do not like the wording of this amendment. I would prefer to have seen an amendment which deplored the government's failure to make a clearcut statement on its intentions with reference to the administration of veterans hospitals, and criticized the government for failing to refer this matter to the veterans affairs committee. However, after listening to the defence which was put up by the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Teillet) I have become convinced I ought to vote in favour of this amendment because the minister, it seems to me, has completely failed to give the house any satisfactory statement with respect to the government's intentions regarding veterans hospitals.
The minister says that this is a very serious problem-and nobody doubts that. He says that he has faced up to the problem. That is like the Irishman saying you should take the bull by the horns and look it straight in the face, because it may turn out to be a wolf in sheep's clothing. To look at the problem and face up to the problem is not enough. We need some statement of the government's solution to the problem. When the minister says that my colleague from Kootenay West is simply suggesting that they make a decision to do nothing, that is not in accordance with the facts. We are asking the government what it is going to do; we want to know what the government is going to do. More important,

we would like to make sure that the minister knows what he is going to do; and certainly there was nothing in his statement today that would indicate that he has any clear idea of what he intends to do about this problem.
The minister said that there is a serious problem and he has outlined it to the house. I take it, first of all, that the problem is not that the veterans hospitals have empty beds and are unoccupied. The minister says, instead, that bed occupancy is running around 75 per cent to 80 per cent capacity. That is normal occupancy for any hospital; anything much higher than that is too crowded for good administration. So there is no problem that there are empty beds or that space is going to waste. The problem is not the lack of good medical care at the present time. The minister says the problem lies in the fact that veterans hospitals in this country, like veterans hospitals in every other country, are gradually changing their function. This is to be expected. In the years immediately following the war, veterans hospitals were largely active treatment centres providing medical, surgical, nursing care and physiotherapy for veterans who had been badly wounded and were in need of active treatment. With the passage of time these hospitals are increasingly adopting a custodial care program of looking after long-stay cases and the chronically ill.
Mr. Speaker, we cannot brush this aside. The function of these hospitals has changed, but the importance of the problem remains, and I suggest to the minister that it will increase; that in the next 10 or 15 years, when the veterans of the last war are getting into their 50's and 60's, there will be a greatly increased number of applicants for admission to veterans hospitals. These will be burnt-out veterans and men who because of their war service will find in their later years that they require long-stay care.
The minister's argument is that because these hospitals have changed the nature of their function, this creates a problem of staff; that it is difficult to keep medical staff, who are naturally more concerned with active treatment care. This does pose a problem and it may mean a change in the kind of staff provided; because let us not delude ourselves, hospitals providing custodial care for the chronically ill need specially trained staff, as is proved by the geriatric centres that are being built in this country. They need the kind of staff that are specially trained to look after these particular kind of people. But the mere fact that these hospitals are changing their function does not mean they are no longer required.
Veterans Hospitals Transfer
What the government has to do, it seems to me, is to decide one of two things. Are these hospitals now going to become almost exclusively custodial care institutions to look after long-stay cases and the chronically ill? If they are, then both the staff and the equipment needs to be changed. The other alternative the government has is this. If these hospitals have such large investments for diagnostic equipment and diagnostic procedures that it would be a shame to waste it, then the policy ought to be to build custodial care institutions, move the veterans into those custodial care institutions, and leave in the present hospitals those who need active treatment-they will be a relatively small number and a diminishing number-and make arrangements to either take in civilians or enter into some arrangement with the local authorities so that active treatment centres can be used by both veterans and the general public.
The minister has made mention of the Saskatoon situation. There a very ideal arrangement has been worked out. In the University hospital space has been set aside and beds are reserved for veterans requiring active treatment. But the important point is that at the same time the government is building a hospital to provide custodial care for the chronically ill veterans; and until the latter is done, nothing can be done about the former. What concerns us is that the minister seems to be charging ahead with a program to dispose of veterans hospitals without telling us where the veteran long-stay cases who are there now are going to be cared for. If they are left in the hospitals they are in now, the hospitals are going to be 75 per cent to 80 per cent full, so where are the civilians going to go? If they are going to be moved out of those hospitals, where are they going to be sent?
I want to tell the minister that turning these hospitals hack to the municipalities and the provincial governments means that all those veterans who are not receiving active treatment will be denied admission, of necessity, because the provincial governments do not provide under their hospital plans-except in one province-for custodial care for the chronically ill. The veterans who are in these hospitals now have to be assured that there is some place for them to go; and we have to be assured that the increasing numbers of veterans who will require long term care will be provided for.
If the minister were coming before this house to say it is the intention of the government to build hospitals to take care of the chronically ill veterans, hospitals that will cost less per bed because less expensive diagnostic equipment will be installed, and that when these institutions have been built

Veterans Hospitals Transfer and the chronically ill veterans have been moved into them this will leave room in the active treatment centres-when that day comes the government is prepared to enter into agreements with the provinces and the municipalities so that whatever space is left in these active treatment hospitals can be made available to civilians, that would make sense; that would be a solution to the problem. But I listened very carefully to the minister this afternoon. He talked about dealing with the problem of each hospital on its merits; of the decision in each case being taken in view of the time, the place and the circumstances. This does not answer anything. Let us take the Colonel Belcher hospital as an example. Are the custodial care veterans in that hospital to be moved? If so, where are they going to go? If they are not going to be moved, then all the problems the minister has outlined concerning the difficulty of getting medical personnel who want to look after active treatment cases and not the chronically ill will still remain.
It seems to me that the minister is going at this whole problem the wrong way. It may be that his department has worked out a plan. If it has, the minister certainly has not outlined it to the house this afternoon. This is why I would support the idea which we have advanced several times during this session, namely that the whole question of veterans hospitals be referred to the veterans affairs committee, where the department can put its plans forward, where the veterans organizations can present their views, and where hospital and medical authorities can give us their opinions on this question. Then whatever the government's plan is, if it is going to continue to look after veterans adequately I am sure the house will go along with it.
We are not anxious to retain ownership or control. It does not seem to me that it is important whether an active treatment hospital is run by the Department of Veterans Affairs and civilians are allowed to use it, and the Department of Veterans Affairs gets paid by the hospital insurance branch; or whether it is vice versa and the municipality operates the hospital with the Department of Veterans Affairs being allocated a given number of beds which are reserved for the use of veterans. I do not think we ought to be arguing about this very minor point.
It seems to me that the important point, a point which appears to have escaped the minister entirely, is that you cannot take veterans out of active treatment hospitals unless you have some place to put them. That means building hospitals for the chronically ill; and until they are built it is simply

absurd to talk of turning these veterans hospitals over to some other body. The government need not think that they can discharge their responsibility by turning these hospitals over to the provinces and the municipalities and then say: "Well, if there are not enough rooms for the veterans you can put the civilians out". Surely that is not a very satisfactory solution.
I want to emphasize a point which I think needs to be reiterated again and again, and that is that chronically ill veterans as they get older need custodial care. There is no place to equal a veterans institution. In the first place most of the provinces and municipalities do not supply that kind of facility anyway under the hospital insurance plan, so there are no facilities for them to go to. But even if there were it is of great importance that these men in their latter years should be able to spend their time in the companionship of their comrades with whom they served in the services. This is something to which they are entitled. It is bad enough for any man to spend years of his life, particularly the declining years, being a semi-invalid; the least we can do is to make those years happy so that he can have the companionship and association of men who have common memories and have had the common experience of serving together in Her Majesty's forces. This is why, before the government talks of getting rid of active treatment hospitals, it seems to me it has to embark upon a program of building hospitals for chronically ill veterans. When those hospitals have been established, if it is found that the number of veterans who need active treatment is relatively small, then the government has the choice either of reserving wings in general hospitals and providing for the care of veterans in those wings, or of turning over the veterans active treatment hospitals to the municipalities and reserving sufficient rooms so that those veterans who need active treatment care can be assured of getting it.

Because after all, Mr. Speaker, this is a very important matter, as the minister himself has said; and I think he understands why the members of this house are concerned. It will be too late to do anything after the minister gets up on the orders of the day and announces that he has just turned over three or four hospitals to municipalities. The door will be closed and we will have embarked upon a policy from which it will be difficult to retreat. Once these hospitals have been turned over it will not be easy for the minister to retrace his steps. Therefore I urge him, before we start down a path that may have an uncertain and an unfortunate ending, to submit this whole question to the veterans affairs committee so that the policy which will emanate from that committee will be carefully considered, will be well thought out, and will be in the best interests of the veterans of this country.

I am interested in this problem. I did not know I would be participating in this debate when yesterday I had a conversation with an amputee who had served with the Hastings-Prince Edward regiment. Anne de Bellevue; the veterans wing of Kingston General; Kingston D.Y.A. hospital; Christie st. hospital; Sunny-brook hospital, and the Tri-Service hospital on Alta Vista road here in Ottawa. I believe all hon. members will agree that conditions do change very radically. In the course of our conversation yesterday at lunch this veteran, who incidentally is carrying on a very good business in the Cornwall area, indicated some of the changes he had seen in the Tri-Service hospital even during the time he had been accepting medical care there. I am sure the veterans across this country are very much indebted to the Department of Veterans Affairs for the extraordinarily high quality, and personal interest, of the service given. I should like to refer hon. members to some of the evidence given in that committee on Tuesday, December 10, 1963. On that occasion Dr. J. N. B. Crawford, the director general of treatment services was called and was subjected to a line of examination, in the first instance, by the hon. member for Kootenay West. Let me just read these questions and answers into the record. Dr. Crawford said:
In June of 1960, I called a conference in Montreal of all chiefs of medical service in all the D.V.A. hospitals. We met here for one or two days and threshed out this problem.
This was a problem in June of 1960.
The consensus at that time was that the high proportion of older men in our hospitals certainly did have an effect on the quality of care which could be given in a hospital that was trying to be a general hospital.
Later, he told the committee:
I then wrote a paper or report for my minister in which I outlined the problem and proposed three possible solutions as I saw them at that time.
This, remember, is June, 1960.
The first was that we would admit to our hospitals a younger patient load.
Some hon. members suggested this as a possible solution.
The second possibility was that we would buy the services we required in the federal government from community hospitals, and in this way there was a possibility that D.V.A. hospitals which were potentially active treatment hospitals might be turned over to suitable agencies.
The third possibility was that we would carry on as we were doing, accepting the fact that we would thereby more and more come to be hospitals for the care of chronic diseases and for the provision of domiciliary care.
He stressed the fact that this meeting took place in the early summer of 1960. Since that time, we have had a number of ministers of veterans affairs. They were Hon. Alfred J. Brooks; Hon. Gordon Churchill and Hon. Marcel Lambert. I think perhaps hon. members of this house would be interested in the rather penetrating comments and questions that were put to the director of treatment services by the last Conservative minister of veterans affairs. Incidentally this hon. gentleman has made a singularly high contribution to this house, certainly in matters of national defence, as speaker and as a man with a good military record of his own; who went through the Dieppe campaign and who was a prisoner of war. I have served for some years as a governor of a hospital and as a member of the board of trustees of a university. As such I have been interested in medical facilities and in the operation of a medical school. As a matter of fact, the dean of the Queen's medical school at this time is Dr. Harry Botterell who cared for me at Basingstoke military hospital in England. I know the record of this man's performance as one of the top ranking neurosurgeons in Canada. After that I was cared for by Colonel Botterell for a time at Christie street and later at Sunny-brook and now it is my good fortune to be able to refer to him again because he is at a university training hospital, Kingston general hospital. He has pointed out repeatedly to the board of trustees of Queen's University the importance of integration of university and hospital facilities. Training and service go together.
What is the real problem we are facing today? Our veterans hospitals are more and more becoming institutions for the treatment or accommodation of the chronically ill. We have been told that 70 per cent of our patient population is now in this category and that the median age of the patient population is 67 years in spite of the 6 per cent of the population made up of young patients drawn from the armed services. What would the situation be, for instance, if it was not policy to send these young soldiers to the D.V.A. hospitals in order to provide some element of active treatment care? Seventy seven per cent of all patients in D.V.A. hospitals now are over 50 years of age.
I think it was the last speaker who commented that there is no place to equal a veterans institution for the care of these people. I want to say, with great respect, that I do not entirely agree with that proposition. One of my dear and respected friends, and a great friend of my father, was Colonel Fred Kemp. I remember going to visit this man many times before 1939. He was seriously wounded in world war I and he had three gallantry awards, including the D.S.O. and bar. This man lived for many years under D.V.A. care before he died. I want to tell the house that I always left that hospital shocked that a man who had been acclaimed as a distinguished hero of the first world war should be living in such circumstances.
The fact is that conditions for the care of veterans did not continue between the wars as we would have liked them to. It is true that we did our best. Often there was paint on the wall but in many cases there was a hunger on the part of veterans to be treated like other people and to have some of the benefit of the good facilities that go with a progressive active service hospital.

Veterans hospitals are beginning to lose their attraction as teaching centres.
I might point out this fact because it is of some importance to people who care about hospitals generally. Ten years ago a young doctor seeking a higher specialist qualification such as F.R.C.S. could take all his required training in a veterans hospital. That is not so today. Today most of our hospitals are approved for only one year of required training. Therefore the tendency is for the candidate to apply in the first instance to a hospital where he can do his complete training.
It has become increasingly difficult to maintain the interest of treatment staff, especially to recruit new medical and nursing staff. Interest can only be maintained, even on the part of physiotherapists, if some way can be found to combine the treatment of veterans with the treatment of a younger age group. In saying this I am in no way suggesting that there is not very great importance attached to domiciliary care. I am simply pointing out the fact that there is a change, and a dynamic and useful ministry of veterans affairs has got to have the courage, notwithstanding the criticisms that will be bound to come to it, to adjust to change and to prepare for change.
As I see it, these changes are not going to occur overnight. I think this debate is a useful one because it is preparing the way, we hope, for a more serious and responsible examination of these problems by the veterans affairs committee in due course. The Brockville Recorder and Times of March 23 last had this to say:
This consternation on the part of the organizations representing veterans is not likely to last, however, when closer scrutiny is given the reasons behind the government's move and just what such a move will mean to veterans.
Veterans affairs minister Teillet and the government are merely following the recommendations of the Glassco commission, a commission authorized by the former Progressive Conservative government. Neither Mr. Teillet, nor the federal Liberal government, are about to betray the veterans as suggested by Gordon Churchill, former Conservative veterans affairs minister. I stress the word "gradual''.
-and those of the general community lay greater hope of obtaining high standards of care for veterans over the long term.

When we look for a solution I think we have got to look deeply at the problem. I assure the hon. member I am not one to believe everything recommended by the Glassco commission. There are parts of the Glassco commission report with which I certainly do not agree. But let me touch on a few of the skeletal conclusions on which the Glassco recommendations are based. They point out that the Canadian expeditionary force in the first world war suffered heavy casualties and accordingly in world war II the government had every reason to expect that the volume of casualties would be larger. The result was that the government undertook a very busy program of renovation and construction so that we now have 11 D.V.A. hospitals scattered across Canada.
It was expected that the casualties of world war II would be substantially more than in the earlier conflict and this assumption proved to be false. However, a program of new hospital construction was undertaken on a large scale and since the end of the war older hospitals have either been replaced or in the main rebuilt. Therefore we now have these 11 veterans institutions with a total capacity of 8,408 beds.

The Glassco commission points out that in the past standards of medical care in these hospitals have been high. They state that the original aim of these hospitals was to provide for the grievously wounded-this touches on the point raised by the hon. member from the N.D.P.-and that therefore many of these hospitals were constructed with specialized surgical facilities and specialized neurosurgical and X-ray facilities. They certainly were not planned as domiciliary in character. What about a little straight talk on this? I happen to have had the distinct honour to have got to know one veteran, and I think this is something that is germane to our discussion. He enlisted on August 21, 1939. He went overseas as an observer-navigator. He flew on 21 missions as navigator in Halifax bombers before being given the special assignment of pathfinder, which as we remember, represented an elite classification in bomber command. He was shot down on his third pathfinder flight between Reims and Chalons-Sur-Marne, not far from the Argonne wood. He was on the loose for two weeks, walking by night and hiding by day.

He spent the balance of the war there, except for the final stages when he, along with many other prisoners, was put on forced marches in the month of January, when his nazi captors were retreating many hundreds of miles in the face of allied advances. Mr. Speaker, I feel I must make a few remarks on this subject. I assure you I will not make many, and first I want to commend the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) upon his very fair and cogent address this afternoon. He put forward the matter of the Colonel Belcher hospital and the feelings of the veterans in a reasonable and precise manner.
I fail to see how veterans on the government side of the house can support the projected turnover of D.V.A. hospitals to other authorities. To hand over any of the facilities that the government of Canada is supposed to maintain for veterans, is definitely giving up their duty and responsibility to the veterans who made it possible for the country to survive even this long.
I speak as a representative of a constituency which contains at least 20 branches of the Canadian Legion, some of which hold numbers as early as 26, 33 and 35. I have had many telegrams from these branches of the Royal Canadian Legion and every one of them demands that the proposed hand-over of veterans hospitals to other organizations be not proceeded with and that everything possible be done to stop it. It may be that in the course of time it may be necessary to hand over certain parts of the responsibility of the government of Canada in this regard to other organizations, but I believe this must be gone into very carefully and very slowly. I just want to quote at this time from the address made yesterday by my hon. friend from Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) in which he stated our outlook on this question. He said, as reported on page 2373 of Hansard:
As I see it, the solution is to let things remain as they are, with such modifications in the care and treatment of our veterans as are acceptable to our medical advisers, to the veterans themselves and to the veterans organizations. If this means making provision for those who do not require active treatment right in the D.V.A. hospitals, then let us make that provision; but to seize on this other course of handing these hospitals over to other control is repugnant to me and is certainly repugnant to the veterans organizations.
That is the paragraph which the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) would not read into the record. He chose to latch on to

some other statement which he said my hon. friend from Winnipeg South Centre had made.
In this proposed hand-over of D.V.A. hospitals I wonder why the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Teillet) did not choose as a guinea pig Deer Lodge military hospital in Winnipeg, in the province from which he himself comes. Why did he choose the province of Alberta and, especially, the Colonel Belcher military hospital in Calgary? While I live some 300 miles away from the city of Calgary, now, my personal interest in the Colonel Belcher hospital is very great. I was one of the earliest patients in that hospital after it was organized and before that I was on the staff of the district depot in Calgary which was the forerunner of the present regional office of the D.V.A. in Alberta. I was there when this hospital was being organized. When the hospital was organized I was a patient and then I was on the staff of that hospital. So my interest in the Colonel Belcher hospital is very great. It was not the hospital then that it is now, because a new building has been provided. But it was the Colonel Belcher military hospital at that time. Even at that time the service there was the very best and I do believe that the idea of turning such hospitals over to other organizations is very wrong, because, as the minister said, even at present beds available in military hospitals are from 75 per cent to 80 per cent occupied.
The trouble seems to be that there is difficulty in getting sufficient staff. Well, as has been pointed out by the minister, the staff of military hospitals receive the same remuneration and have the same working conditions as, or perhaps better working conditions than those in many hospitals which are not D.V.A. hospitals. For the life of me I cannot see why it should be so difficult to recruit medical staff, that is, doctors and nurses, for these hospitals. The minister mentioned something about second class medical treatment which might be available later on. That is something I fail to understand, because the doctors and the nurses who enlist for work in military hospitals are dedicated people. They dedicate their lives to this great service, and people whose lives are dedicated do not provide second class service for anybody.
The minister also maintained that the situation is different in every part of Canada. I do not agree with that statement at all. Wherever you have a veteran in Canada, that veteran is in practically every case a man who had volunteered for service. This service was rendered without any idea of reward and it is the duty of the government of Canada to look after such people when they

need treatment. There can be no question about that. Handing over the medical services and the hospitals available to our veterans is just no good, because you cannot expect those who are looking after sick people to give the same consideration to everybody as they do to operative cases; and so many of these veterans are not now operative cases.
The veterans who will require hospital treatment are likely to increase in numbers in the next few years for the simple reason that the veterans of the second world war are now reaching middle age, and the results of their active service will begin to show, whether they were wounded or not; the results of the privations they suffered will begin to show. As for the veterans of the first world war, there are not as many of us left as there were. A great many will require treatment. This is not likely to be operative treatment, and where and how is this care to be arranged if we do not retain our D.V.A. hospitals?
There is no provision for the domiciliary care of veterans who are disabled, except in some places. The area which I represent is contiguous to the city of Edmonton. In that city there is not a veterans hospital. The veterans at the university hospital receive treatment in the Mewburn pavilion, and that pavilion is staffed by D.V.A. doctors. All the arrangements with regard to hospitalization are made and provided by the University of Alberta hospital, which is a child of the provincial government of Alberta. I have received a great many complaints about the provisions for hospitalization in that hospital, but I have yet to receive even one complaint about the medical or nursing attention. The complaint is with regard to the arrangements of the hospital and the lack of attention to veterans who are perhaps not operative cases. This is something that I believe could happen in all hospitals which may not be operated by the D.V.A.
I think that in the proposed turnover of these hospitals at this time the government is just trying to run before it walks. It is not making any provision for what is going to happen in the future, and the veterans would just be forced to take their chance on being looked after properly. I therefore am wholly in support of the amendment that has been moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) and I think every veteran in this house should also be in accord with that amendment.
I remarked when I began my speech, Mr. Speaker, that I would only say a few words.
I have been longer than I intended to be, but I have said things that I believe must be said, and must be said by a person who is a long time veteran.

Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to have an opportunity to speak in this debate. I would like to say right away that, as a veteran, although I agree with some of the things that have been said during this debate from the other side of the house, I am not in favour of this amendment and I plan to vote against it. I will outline my reasons as I proceed, although I do not expect to speak for very long because I know there are others who have important things to say. However, Mr. Speaker, there are a few points that I wish to make.
First of all, I am a member of the veterans affairs committee and am concerned, having had the experience in that committee of a great deal of good will and free exchange of opinion, that this amendment will prejudice that good will by making this a political issue, that it most certainly is not. I think all of us on this side of the house, as well as those on the other side, are trying to do our utmost to look after the best interests of our veterans. I for one am satisfied from what the minister has said that our policy is to provide the best possible care for veterans even if this means making changes. I am also convinced that part of our policy is to consult with the veterans when the right time arrives.
My particular concern in this matter, apart from being a member of the veterans affairs committee, is that I have a veterans hospital in my riding, the Victoria veterans hospital. I can say from various studies I have made of this hospital that in my part of the country we are going to be in the veterans business for a long, long time to come, I would say probably longer than any other part of the nation, because the statistics show that, for one reason or another-and I believe it is because of the temperate climate which we enjoy out there-veterans from other parts of Canada gravitate towards Victoria in their later years. The census taken in 1961 shows that of all the male veteran population over 30 years of age, those living in the Victoria riding represent the highest percentage of anywhere in Canada; 42 per cent of all the male population over the age of 30 in the vicinity of Victoria are veterans. When we break this down even further, we see in the higher age groups, those of 65 years of age or over, once again we have the highest percentage in Canada. From age 60 to 64, 46 per cent are veterans; from 65 to 69, 53 per cent are veterans. This compares with a nationwide average of about 25 per cent to 28 per cent. So I am very, very concerned, Mr. Speaker, with the matter of veterans hospitals and their future.

Veterans Hospitals Transfer In view of the figures which I have just given to the house, I would like to say that I agree with many of the points raised by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas), particularly with respect to the chronically ill or domiciliary care patients. In some parts of the country this figures is as low as 8 per cent. However, it is not in every part of the country that the veterans hospital is fortunate enough to have a large public hospital immediately adjacent to it. We do. We have for some time been sharing some of our facilities between the veterans hospital and the public hospital, and to our mutual advantage. It is this sort of thing that I would like to see investigated, to see whether there is not some further advantage to be gained for the veterans by more of this type of co-operation. For example, the D.V.A. hospital in Victoria already uses the facilities of the Royal Jubilee hospital for the treatment of cancer. We use their psychiatric clinic, and they provide emergency services and share their laboratory facilities.
This is the sort of thing I should like to investigate in my riding to the benefit of all the veterans. It has been explained to me that there is all sorts of room for this type of co-operation. I am told that new techniques are being developed in medicine which require not only expensive equipment but also, and much more importantly, highly skilled and trained teams of doctors and nurses to operate the equipment. I fully realize there is no one in this house who would wish to deny the veterans the full advantage of the use of this type of equipment in an emergency. I know we would all vote the money to acquire such equipment, but we cannot vote the experience that these teams require. These teams have to be put together, and having been introduced to the equipment have to use the equipment and use it frequently so that they know how to
[Mr. Groos.l
use it properly when the time comes. I think that most doctors will agree with me when I say that these teams cannot be duplicated in every hospital across the country. It is much better to have a highly skilled team in one central position and to make it available to veterans when the time comes. This is the sort of thing I am looking for in any revision of our plans for veterans hospitals.
I do not want to take up too much time this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, but I should like to make two or three other points. An attempt has been made today to show that all veterans are against any change in policy.
I do not think this is so. However, I must confess I have sympathy with the veterans who are not aware of what changes the government have in mind. I am also in sympathy with the minister, who cannot possibly approach the veterans with the changes which he has in mind until he has been able to consult with all the individual hospitals and work out solutions for each individual case so that he can present his plans to the veterans.
When I have explained this matter to the veterans groups in my riding they have accepted it in the way I would have expected.
I have received over 1,300 cards from veterans as well as a number of letters from veterans organizations in my riding. These cards read:
I,	the undersigned, a veteran, protest the handing over of the Victoria veterans hospital to any other administration.
I think hon. members will agree with me that 1,300 cards all worded exactly alike are some sign of an organized protest, and it is the kind of protest I welcome because it is the type of information which a member of parliament needs to show how the people are thinking. It is interesting to note that of the 1,300 letters I have received there are signs that perhaps this highly organized campaign is being a little over-organized. A number of these protests have been duplicated. Some people have sent in two or three protests bearing the same name and address, and I have had over 50 of my replies returned marked "Not known at this address". I tried to reply to these letters straight away when they first came in at the rate of some 200 or 300 a day, and I think I have replied to over 1,000 of them.
I might also point out that a number of these cards have been sent to me with the word "protest" crossed out and the word "favour" inserted instead, so that the card would read:
I,	the undersigned, a veteran, favour the handing over of the Victoria veterans hospital to any other administration.

Or it might read:
I, the undersigned, a veteran, applaud the handing over of the Victoria veterans hospital to any other administration.
However, I do not attach any particular significance to this sort of thing, Mr. Speaker, other than that it goes to show that this objection is not a unanimous one. 1 have had letters from veterans who take the sane and sensible view, which I think is shared by many hon. members of this house on both sides, that it is time that at least a study was made of this problem so as to find out whether some changes should be made which would be of advantage to the veterans in some parts of the country. That is all we are looking for; at least that is all I am looking for. I want better care for our veterans, and I know of no one who will disagree with me on that.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that we can provide better care. One of the complaints that a veteran makes at the moment is that when he arrives at a veterans hospital he cannot always have his own doctor because the doctor concerned is not an accredited doctor at that hospital. It is surely better for a patient undergoing surgery in a hospital to have his own doctor who is well acquainted with the case. Then there is also the question of equipment to which I have referred. This new, highly technical equipment could be made available on a joint basis at a number of hospitals.
I should like to come back to the remarks made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, because I said that I agreed with a great deal of what he said. He was talking about domiciliary care. This is care which is in the main given to the older veterans, who comprise primarily the world war I group. All of these men have our profound sympathy. However, what I should like to see as a result of this debate is some clarification of the position of those undergoing domiciliary care. There is the suspicion that they are being treated only on sufferance, and I think that this suspicion must be removed. In particular, I think of the case of world war I veterans who fought under really awful, almost inconceivable conditions for months and months on end. There is no doubt, whether or not they were wounded, that this country owes them all a debt which we can never repay; and I for one wish to see them looked after in their old age even if it means that we have to provide domiciliary quarters for them under the operation of the Department of Veterans Affairs.
I have been making investigations in Victoria with the local groups to see whether or not this can be done. As has been pointed out
Veterans Hospitals Transfer on more than one occasion, the veterans are a very understanding group. They know perfectly well that it would be better for everyone concerned if, instead of occupying beds in a hospital each of which costs somewhere around $25,000 a year to maintain, they were occupying beds much more suitable for their circumstances, namely those designed for domiciliary-type care. Although I cannot say I have achieved any result yet, I am exploring the possibility of taking the lead and attempting to establish the groundwork for the provision of this type of domiciliary accommodation in Victoria. What a fine thing this would be for the veterans. What a fine thing this would be for the community, and for Canada. It would be wonderful if this type of accommodation were made possible through the three various levels of government.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the difficult position the minister is facing has been amply demonstrated here by the various suggestions that have been put forward by the various members from both sides of the house as to how he should accomplish his purpose. This demonstrates to me the extent of the problem. I want to say again that I am satisfied our policy is to provide the best possible care for veterans, even if this means making changes. I do not believe there are any members in this house who will disagree with that policy.
