Mr. Speaker, we have had a very interesting debate occasioned by the introduction of the amendment with regard to the possible transfer of veterans hospitals to provincial and municipal control. I say it has been an interesting debate, and I think it is understandable that varied feelings and convictions should be indicated in the discussion of a subject such as this one. I have followed with special interest the statements and interventions of those who have served in the armed forces. Some of us were not in that particular role, but possibly in roles that the national government considered essential to the successful prosecution of the war effort. Since we are dealing with veterans, as I say, I have been especially interested in listening to those who have served and who have expressed their views with regard to the matter now before us.
Possibly the first indication we had that something was moving in this regard was the report of the Glassco commission. This has been brought to our attention also and the various sections of it have been placed

Veterans Hospitals Transfer on the record tor public information. I believe, as was pointed out, that we must remember this was a task that was committed to the Glassco commission based almost wholly upon economic considerations. We are called upon to temper a report based purely upon economic considerations with the human elements that are involved in a situation such as the one now before us. Mention has been made of the announced policy or lack of policy indicated by the Minister of Veterans Affairs. I believe possibly he has to be blamed for not making forthright statements in this house in answer to the many questions that have been asked and the many submissions that have been made.
We waited for a long time before any statement was made outlining government policy. When that statement was made I fear that in many respects it was rather inconclusive, rather indefinite and left us very much in the dark regarding the policy the government intended to put into effect. When the minister made his statement on March 16, he outlined three main considerations that were to be kept in mind in relation to this important matter. As reported at page 930 of Hansard for March 16, the minister said:
These conditions, three in number, are as follows: First, accommodation for the treatment of service connected disabilities among veterans must be immediately available at all times, and treatment must be provided in accordance with standards prescribed by the Department of Veterans Affairs. Second, community institutions of acceptable standards must be available to look after the work load created by other classes of veterans, which means that such veterans will be able to obtain treatment in their own communities, near their own friends and families. Finally, satisfactory arrangements must be made for the continued employment of professional and other staffs now serving in our institutions.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that these considerations are very commendable, but as pointed out this afternoon, it would seem to me that specific steps must be indicated to ensure that these safeguards can be implemented and our veterans will continue to receive the high standard of service and treatment that they have received up to this time. We have all received communications with regard to this matter. I, personally, have received communications from various branches urging that we oppose any attempt to make this transfer of D.V.A. hospitals to other agencies.
A letter appeared in the April issue of The Legionary and it was directed to the Minister of Veterans Affairs by Mr. D. M. Thompson, dominion secretary of the Royal Canadian Legion. He had been instructed to convey to the minister certain requests. I am not going to read the letter, but I am going to read the requests that are made.

(1)	That no action be taken by the government in regard to the handing over of D.V.A. hospitals until the Royal Canadian Legion has had an opportunity to discuss this problem further with you;
(2)	That you give a definite statement on government policy regarding these hospitals and the provision for future treatment for Canadian veterans;
(3)	That this statement indicate clearly the government's future policy as it will apply to treatment provided under each of the general classification sections of the veterans treatment regulations;
(4)	That when this statement has been received and studied, the dominion president and elected officers of the Royal Canadian Legion be given an opportunity to meet with you and discuss this entire matter.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we are aware of the dangers that are inherent in such proposals as have been advanced. We can understand very well the fears of the veterans and those who are responsible for the welfare of the veterans. We can appreciate their fears. We would urge the minister, therefore, to go slowly in the implementation of these proposals which he has outlined or on the proposals that have been outlined by the Glassco commission. As I pointed out, the Glassco commission was operating from the point of view of economic considerations. I am sure the minister recognizes the fact, as does every member in this house, that the human element must be taken into consideration in the issue which is currently before us.
I suggest, therefore, that the government and the minister move very slowly in the implementation of this policy. Above all, I believe discussions should continue with the veterans organizations. We should try to reconcile their problems, dispel their fears and allay their suspicions that when the matter is finally proceeded with it will be with the knowledge that the veterans organizations have a clear understanding of what the minister has in mind, and the veterans will be assured that the treatment they may require in the future will be available at the time it is required.
As I have said, we have listened to veterans on both sides of the house and, as was pointed out today, the minister himself has a very laudable service record. The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) also spoke, as well as members of the official opposition and others on this side of the house. All of these hon. members have laudable service records. Yet we see how widely divergent their views are with respect to this problem.
I do not think we can charge the government with being oblivious to the needs of the veterans. I do not think we can charge members of the opposition with making this matter purely a political football. I think we must credit each and every member with a sincere motivation so far as this question is concerned.

I simply wish to point out the fact that the veterans themselves hold widely divergent views with respect to this problem.
I think this points up very clearly the importance of further negotiations and discussions in an endeavour to resolve the problem and find some common ground of understanding before we proceed in this fashion. Once again I urge, as I did on a previous occasion when this matter was first broached by the minister, that the committee on veterans affairs be seized with this problem. The committee can then call before it members of veterans organizations and others who want to present opinions, suggestions and proposals. I believe that in this way we can resolve the problems involved and find a satisfactory solution to them.
I do not believe that this matter should involve a want of confidence motion so far as the government is concerned. I think this is a rather radical and drastic step because I believe that through co-operation and the pooling of the suggestions, knowledge and understanding of those who are vitally concerned we can arrive at a satisfactory solution, one which will, as I have said, allay the fears of the veterans and still provide for any change in the administrative field that is considered vital and important at this time.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in support of the amendment of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill). I am prompted to do so for three reasons, first, because of my medical training, second, because of the great number of veterans who have written me and sent me telegrams as well as communications even from civilians and, third, because I believe the veterans hospitals across Canada are serving a very useful function in looking after our veterans and are also doing great work in the field of research.
We have in Canada today over 200,000 veterans who are entitled to treatment. There are approximately 8,500 beds in the 11 veterans hospitals across Canada and when we look at the record we find that there were approximately 75,000 admissions last year which produced a case load of approximately 80 per cent usage of available hospital beds. This is a reasonable average considering that the length of stay of the veterans was approximately three weeks.
I also want to emphasize that the veterans hospitals are well equipped. On the basis of knowledge I can refer to Sunnybrook, and on the basis of advice received to Shaugh-nessy. They not only have the finest of equipment, but in the case of Sunnybrook members of the staff are associated with the
Business of the House
University of Toronto. Their staffs are the finest in Canada. These hospitals are doing a tremendous job not only in the work they are carrying on but in the training of young doctors who go forth with excellent training to treat people across the country.
The veterans in these hospitals make ideal cases for study and treatment. They can be given the most modern medical and surgical treatment in these hospitals but, above all, their cases can be followed up over the years to see what the results of the treatment may be, which may be very difficult in respect of the civilian population. The veterans are also unique in relation to the civilian population in that most of them have suffered the stresses and strains of war. Many of them have hidden injuries that do not appear until years later. They are a special group of people because the civilian population has not undergone the hidden stresses and strains of war. Only a veterans hospital with a veterans outlook and staffed by people such as work in these institutions will have the proper perspective to look after these people and give them the best treatment.
I want to refer for a few minutes to the general hospitals. General hospitals are active treatment hospitals. Their patients stay from 10 to 12 days, I suppose, but they are active treatment hospitals in that the cases they de'al with involve people who are acutely ill medically or who need emergency operations or who have been involved in accidents. I would remind the house that 12 per cent of all the beds in general hospitals today are occupied by accident cases. Today most of our veterans are over 35 years of age.

Mr. Speaker, before the house adjourned at six o'clock I had stated that veterans hospitals were well equipped and that they were well staffed. For example, the Sunnybrook hospital has many excellently trained men, and I had stated its consulting staff was of the highest professional skill and training, that the hospital carried on with well kept records, a great deal of scientific research, that young graduates in medicine received a splendid internship there, and that the veterans received the most modern treatment they could have anywhere in Canada in an environment suitable to them.
I might have added further that many teaching postgraduate courses have been held there, which have brought in doctors from many hundreds of miles away, and all the doctors I have talked to have stated these were fine teaching courses and were of great benefit to them in their practices.
Now, having said this, I want to draw a distinction again between active treatment hospitals, as general hospitals are, that deal with the acutely ill both medically and surgically, and 12 per cent of whose beds are taken by accident cases and, on the other hand, treatment hospitals for those chronically ill, either surgically, medically or mentally. Mr. Speaker, I would like you to consider that between the ages of five to 35 years the biggest cause of illness and death is accidents.


After the age of 35 the picture changes and we find that people suffer cardio-vascular diseases, cancer, and rheumatic disorders, and other chronic disease. In Canada today we have 1,400,000 people with heart conditions, 350,000 of whom are seriously handicapped, and 72,000 of whom die annually from this disease. Cancer is the next biggest killer, claiming 50 per cent of all its victims. It is not good enough, to write off half of all its victims. Rheumatism and arthritic diseases affect over another one million people, 285,000 of whom are handicapped and 63,000 of whom are hopelessly crippled.
I could go on to state that custodial care is not good enough or adequate enough for a record like this, when we have those great killers striking people after the age of 35 years. We have a population including veterans that is gradually getting older and we must funnel our research and efforts into those cases we are likely going to get anyway.
There must be a constant struggle to achieve the best methods of treatment. Custodial care should be reserved only for those who have no hope of cure. General hospitals have recognized this and have constructed their own arthritic, physiotherapy and mental units close to or as part of the hospital. We require more and more chronic disease beds, and more active treatment going on all the time, if we are to control disease in a population that is constantly getting older, with more people moving into the age group above 35 years.
Veterans hospitals play a very important role in this phase of research and treatment. Let us keep the veterans in their own hospitals, within their own environment. Surely those who went into the army, navy or air force and took the chance of giving their all, and who bear the scars of their adventures, should get the best treatment possible in the best environment it is possible to give them. This will give them the best chance of recovery, by providing them with a happy environment among their old pals who understand them and who fought with them.
This is their right. This is their due, and all of us will not only feel that justice is being done but that some research carried out in those institutions may in the long run save the lives of many human beings. The veterans are entitled to have consideration. In the troubled world of today, the world of the cold wars, we have Canadian troops in quite a few places overseas. Just recently we sent troops to Cyprus, and on more than one occasion it has been suggested that Canadian troops adopt a greater police role. This means, in the event of the outbreak of conflict, that we may need more and more hospital beds.

Therefore I appeal to hon. members, regardless of their political affiliations, for a reconsideration of the rights of veterans across Canada. It is not true to say that we have lots of beds available for them in general hospitals. This is evident right across the country, and it is a complete hoax to say otherwise. The veterans must be treated in their own hospitals and given the best treatment possible.

Mr. Speaker, in the two or three minutes available to me I would like to add my voice to the veterans organizations urging the support and maintenance of our veterans hospitals. The minister may not be aware of why we have these hospitals, but each veteran is, because he figures that the hospitals operated by the Department of Veterans Affairs are ones that were promised to him. These are not hospitals in the true sense of some civic administration, and civic authorities are not capable of operating them.
At one time I was in the old Christie street hospital and I know some people who spent their lifetime in it. They felt it was not a hospital but a home to them. The minister may be a separatist; he may be one of these Liberals who believe in dividing everything up, but I am not.
I believe that as long as we are Canadians we have a responsibility toward those who served us in two world wars and who may be asked to serve again in the future. We have to honour our commitments. Everybody knows that commitments which were undertaken by the previous government were honoured by the minister who was in office at that time. But the hon. gentleman who now holds office is not honouring them; he is entering into arrangements with the provinces and municipalities rather than face up to the task. He has an obligation in terms of the unity of this nation and of the veterans charter, to bring his proposal before the veterans affairs committee. I venture to suggest he has done more thinking about this problem in the last two days than he has done in all the time previous to this debate.
I know some people are committed in this house to voting with a particular object in mind, such as whether to sustain the government. I am pleased, Mr. Speaker, to participate in this debate briefly this evening since the problems created by a lack of transportation facilities have been of major concern to Nova Scotia for many years. Due to Nova Scotia's slow but certain economic growth, these problems have been further aggravated in recent years and it is now evident that further steps must be taken to provide additional transportation links for our expanding fishing industry, secondary manufacturing industry and our tourist industry.
My grievance tonight, therefore, deals with marine transportation problems which face our genial minister who represents one of the maritime constituencies. As many of you are aware, Nova Scotia is almost an island. When the Chignecto canal and power complex is built, we will be actually surrounded by water. However, despite our geographical handicaps, Nova Scotia is going forward.

In 1963 the province's crown corporation negotiated the establishment of 11 new industries, three of which were from outside Canada. Our province became the first one on the continent to produce European motor vehicles when Volvo of Sweden announced its decision to locate an assembly plant at Dartmouth; a British company chose Truro as its home for a new carpet manufacturing plant and the Canada Cement Company began construction of a new plant at Brookfield near Truro. We have a heavy water plant to be built near Glace Bay and new fish processing plants are under way at Lunenburg and Canso. Mineral explorations have been intensified and there has been an increasing awareness of the annual value of between $75 million and $100 million of the province's forest resources. All these projects represent additions to our regional capacity in the primary and secondary industries, but despite this progress we still have a high unemployment rate in the Atlantic provinces which indicate we cannot rest on our oars, and still more must be done if we are to reach the level of prosperity enjoyed by other parts of Canada.
Two things in my opinion must be done to bring this about. First, an immense effort is necessary on the part of industry in cooperation with our provincial and federal governments if our economic lag is to be overcome. Only money, huge amounts of investment capital, can do this. Massive investments over the next decade is the prime requirement. Of course, money alone is not enough. Many human qualities must be added, qualities of judgment, industry, ambition and enterprise. We have these qualities to a great degree in our people but they cannot succeed without investment capital. Here is where the federal government can enter the picture, by improving the transportation needs of our provinces.
We need a second ferry between Nova Scotia and New England to bring us closer to the vast market to the south of us. There is every economic justification for this second ferry at the present time. Here we are in Nova Scotia with average incomes lower by one third than those of the rest of Canada, with double the unemployment and half the capital investment per capita for the remainder of Canada. We have a growing labour force and everywhere mechanization tends to reduce the number of jobs available. Mr. Speaker, when I asked my question on the orders of the day this afternoon on behalf of superannuated civil servants I did so on the basis of one sentence which appears at page 2389 of yesterday's Hansard. At that point there is recorded in Hansard the Prime Minister's telegram of April 16 to the premiers of the provinces concerning the revised Canada pension plan. One of the additions to the Canada pension plan in its new form, and a welcome addition, is spelled out in this sentence:
Benefits in payment would be adjusted to changes in the cost of living, subject to a maximum increase of 2 per cent in any year.
My question therefore this afternoon, and my question tonight is quite straightforward. In view of the fact that the government has now accepted the principle that pensions that have been put in payment should subsequently be increased if the cost of living goes up, will the government apply this principle to its own superannuated civil servants? As the government knows, this is a question I have raised in this house a good many times during the past two decades. The answers have a certain monotony about them. The answer generally is that the matter


is under consideration. On March 6 of this year the Minister of Finance put it this way: As I have said on other occasions, the matter is under consideration all the time.
A few days ago I asked the Prime Minister if he had received a letter from the federal superannuates national association asking for legislation in this session to amend the Public Service Pension Adjustment Act. The Prime Minister replied that he thought he had received this letter, and he said that the matter would be given consideration and that a report would be made to the house as soon as possible. The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that this kind of answer has been made month in and month out for a great many years.
The only time there has ever been any increase in the pensions of civil servants already retired was during the regime of the last Conservative government which put on the statute books the Public Service Pension Adjustment Act. The Liberals in their previous incarnation, and the Liberals in this incarnation, have never done anything to improve the pensions of civil servants already retired. They have improved the civil service pension legislation for persons still employed, and they have made other pension improvements. Hov/ever, so far as civil servants already retired are concerned, there has been nothing done for them.
We have been told to wait for the Canada pension plan. We are glad to see it being improved. We know, however, that the Canada pension plan, even in its best form, will not provide any increase in the pensions of persons already retired. This goes for superannuated civil servants, because no provision has yet been made for these people.
Will the government, having now accepted the principle that pensions that have been started should subsequently be increased if the cost of living goes up, be consistent? When is the government going to play fair with these retired civil servants? When is it going to quit asking these people to wait and wait? When is it going to apply this principle and increase the pensions of retired civil servants, which it can do by amending the Public Service Pension Adjustment Act or in any other way it deems fit?

subtopic: SUPERANNUATED FEDERAL
speechtext:
First of all, I should like to apologize to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre on behalf of the Minister of Finance, who is at a dinner in honour of the prime minister of Trinidad and Tobago.
The government reviews from time to time the question of whether any special action needs to be taken to revise the pensions being paid to superannuated civil servants. It

will be recalled that some increases were authorized under an appropriation act in 1958 and under the Public Service Pension Adjustment Act of 1959. These were not an integral part of the superannuation plan and were not a contractual obligation of the government to its employees or former employees as are benefits payable under the Superannuation Act.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is to be congratulated for raising this question so quickly after the Prime Minister's announcement concerning the Canada pension plan.
It will be realized that retired civil servants, as others, have benefited from the several increases in the old age security pension that have been made in recent years. This has to be taken into account in considering the effect on their pension position of the increases in the cost of living in the past decade. In the short space of time available tonight I cannot give a full analysis of the situation. I can say, however, that the government has had no opportunity to consider the situation with respect to retired civil servants in view of the proposed Canada pension plan legislation.
I should add that the acceptance of the principle of adjustment for the pensions to be payable under a general pension plan for all Canadians does not necessarily imply that

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: SUPERANNUATED FEDERAL
speechtext: It ought to.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: SUPERANNUATED FEDERAL
speechtext: In particular, it cannot be held as necessarily implying that the benefits paid under the superannuation act, which are broadly speaking much more generous than the pensions received by most retired employees in Canada, will be adjusted in this way when those retired under other pension plans cannot anticipate any such comparable adjustment. When the Canada pension plan is passed by this parliament and one can appraise the situation of those who will come under it, the situation of retired civil servants will be reviewed again and we will see whether a legitimate case can be made on the grounds I have mentioned.
